To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of allografts with hepatitis B core antibody positive donors in combination with lamivudine and intravenous HBIgs is an acceptable strategy in liver transplantation.
we have demonstrated that it is safe to use livers from donors with HBsAg and anti‐HBc antibodies.

the combined prophylactic therapy with intravenous HBI and lamivudine is effective in the prevention de novo HBV infections in patients receiving livers from HBcAb‐positive donors, and the HBV‐PCR in serum and lymphocyte is a useful method for monitoring HBV infection in the early stage of the disease.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our approach is reasonably safe and very effective in the prophylaxis of de novo HB infection after liver transplantation from HBV‐DNA‐negative hepatitis B core antibody donors.

the combined prophylactic protocol is safe, effective, and should be considered as the first option in the treatment of patients with end‐stage liver disease who require liver transplantation and who have hepatitis B virus infection.

the risk of transmission of HBV infection from hepatitis B core‐positive donors to recipients of orthotopic liver transplantation is very low, if the donor organs are free of HBV‐DNA and if the recipient receives prophylactic treatment with lamivudine and HBIg for a short period of time (less than 2 weeks).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we can use livers from donors with hepatitis‐B‐core antibodies in liver transplantation without any risk of HBV infection in the recipients.
we have shown that livers from donors who have antibodies against hepatitis B core antigen (HBcAg) are safe for transplantation to patients without hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

the combination of lamivudin and hepatitis B immune globulin for 7 days in patients receiving livers from donors with hepatitis core antibody and negative for HBV DNA is effective in preventing de novo HBV infections after liver transplantation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is safe to use allografts with hepatitis B core antibody positive donors, and that it is possible to prevent the transmission of the virus.

the use of livers from hepatitis‐B core antibody‐positive (HBcAb+) donors for transplantation into hepatitis‐B surface antibody‐negative recipients can be performed safely and effectively with the use of combined prophylaxis (intravenous hepatitis‐B immunoglobulin and lamivudine).
we have developed a safe approach to prevent de novo HBV infections.
